title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
text:
2.1 Types of Issuers
Different issuer types usually trade at different spreads because investors assign different risks and legal protections to each sector.
Common issuer categories include:

sovereign governments,
government agencies,
supranational institutions,
municipalities,
financial corporations,
industrial corporations,
utilities,
structured finance issuers,
mortgage-backed security issuers.

Treasury securities usually define the lowest-yielding benchmark in the domestic currency because they are backed by the sovereign taxing authority and are highly liquid. Corporate bonds trade at positive spreads because investors require compensation for default risk, downgrade risk, and lower liquidity.






NoteIssuer Spread Example



Assume the 10-year Treasury yield is 4.00%. Three 10-year bonds trade at:



Issuer type
Yield
Spread over Treasury




Federal agency
4.35%
35 bps


Utility company
4.95%
95 bps


High-yield industrial company
7.25%
325 bps



The spread increases as investors require more compensation for credit and liquidity risk.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
text:
2.2 Perceived Creditworthiness of Issuer
Creditworthiness is the market’s assessment of the issuer’s ability and willingness to make promised payments. It depends on:

leverage,
earnings stability,
cash-flow coverage,
asset quality,
business risk,
industry cyclicality,
legal protections for creditors,
recovery value if default occurs.

Credit ratings summarize some of this information, but market spreads often react faster than ratings. A widening spread can signal that investors are demanding more compensation for default or downgrade risk.






NoteCredit Spread Example



A 7-year A-rated bond trades at 85 bps over Treasuries. A similar BBB-rated bond from the same sector trades at 145 bps. The 60 bps difference reflects the market’s higher required compensation for the weaker credit profile.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
text:
2.3 Inclusion of Options
Embedded options change a bond’s cash flows and therefore affect its spread.
A callable bond gives the issuer the right to redeem the bond before maturity. This is valuable to the issuer and costly to the investor. If interest rates fall, the issuer can call the bond and refinance at a lower rate, limiting the investor’s price upside.
A putable bond gives the investor the right to sell the bond back to the issuer at a specified price. This is valuable to the investor and costly to the issuer.
All else equal:

callable bonds usually trade at higher yields than otherwise comparable noncallable bonds,
putable bonds usually trade at lower yields than otherwise comparable nonputable bonds,
convertible bonds may trade at lower yields because the conversion option has value.







NoteCallable Bond Example



Suppose two 10-year bonds are issued by the same company:



Bond
Yield
Interpretation




Noncallable
5.40%
No issuer call option


Callable after 3 years
5.80%
Investor requires 40 bps more



The extra yield compensates investors for call risk and reinvestment risk.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
text:
2.4 Taxability of Interest
Tax treatment affects after-tax yield. Investors compare bonds based on what they keep after taxes, not only the quoted pretax yield.
For a taxable bond:
\[
\text{After-tax yield} = y_{\text{taxable}}(1 - t),
\]
where \(t\) is the investor’s marginal tax rate.
For a tax-exempt municipal bond, investors often compute the taxable-equivalent yield:
\[
\text{Taxable-equivalent yield} = \frac{y_{\text{tax-exempt}}}{1 - t}.
\]






NoteTaxable-Equivalent Yield Example



A municipal bond yields 3.00% and the investor’s marginal tax rate is 35%.
\[
\text{Taxable-equivalent yield} = \frac{0.0300}{1 - 0.35} = 0.0462.
\]
The municipal bond is equivalent to a taxable bond yielding 4.62% for this investor.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
text:
2.5 Expected Liquidity of an Issue
Liquidity is the ability to buy or sell a bond quickly, in size, and at low transaction cost. Less liquid bonds usually require higher yields.
Liquidity depends on:

issue size,
dealer inventory,
trading frequency,
transparency of market prices,
eligibility for major indexes,
whether the bond is newly issued or seasoned,
investor concentration.

The liquidity premium is often small in calm markets but can become large during stress.






NoteLiquidity Example



Two BBB-rated bonds have the same maturity and similar credit risk. Bond A is a $2 billion benchmark issue that trades daily. Bond B is a $150 million issue that rarely trades. If Bond A trades at 140 bps and Bond B trades at 175 bps over Treasuries, the 35 bps difference may largely reflect liquidity.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
text:
2.6 Financeability of an Issue
Financeability refers to how easily a bond can be financed in the repo or secured financing market. A bond that can be financed cheaply and reliably is more attractive to leveraged investors.
Financeability depends on:

whether the bond is accepted as collateral,
the repo rate on the bond,
the haircut required by lenders,
settlement reliability,
whether the issue is special in the repo market,
how easily the position can be rolled.

If a bond is difficult to finance, investors may require a higher yield. If it is easy to finance, especially at favorable repo rates, investors may accept a lower yield.






NoteFinanceability Example



A hedge fund can finance Treasury Bond A at a repo rate of 4.00% with a 2% haircut. A less liquid corporate bond requires a 15% haircut and a repo rate of 5.50%. Even if both bonds have attractive yields, the corporate bond consumes more capital and has higher financing risk, so its required spread must be higher.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
text:
2.7 Term to Maturity
Spreads often vary with maturity. The pattern of spreads across maturities is called the credit spread curve.
For high-quality issuers, longer maturities often trade at wider spreads because there is more time for credit quality to deteriorate. For distressed issuers, the spread curve may invert because near-term default risk is more severe than long-term risk.








Figure 2: Illustrative spread curves for high-quality and distressed issuers.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
text:
3.1 Yield Curve
A yield curve plots yields against maturities. The most common version is the Treasury yield curve, which plots yields on Treasury securities from short maturities to long maturities.
Yield curves may be:

upward sloping,
flat,
inverted,
humped.









Figure 3: Common yield curve shapes.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
section: 3.2 Why the Yield Curve Should Not Be Used to Price a Bond
text:
3.2 Why the Yield Curve Should Not Be Used to Price a Bond
A coupon bond has multiple cash flows. A single yield-to-maturity applies one discount rate to all cash flows, but the market may require different discount rates for different cash-flow dates.
If a 5-year bond pays coupons every six months, it has 10 cash flows. The first coupon should be discounted using a 6-month rate, the second coupon using a 1-year rate, and so on. Using only the 5-year yield ignores the fact that the earlier cash flows are less risky with respect to time.
The correct discounting approach is:
\[
P = \sum_{t=1}^{n} \frac{CF_t}{(1 + z_t)^t},
\]
where \(z_t\) is the spot rate for maturity \(t\).






NoteWhy One Yield Can Misprice a Bond



Consider a 2-year annual-pay bond with $50 coupon payments and $1,000 principal. Suppose the 1-year spot rate is 3% and the 2-year spot rate is 5%.
Correct spot-rate price:
\[
P = \frac{50}{1.03} + \frac{1050}{1.05^2} = 1000.65.
\]
If an investor incorrectly discounts both cash flows at the 2-year rate:
\[
P = \frac{50}{1.05} + \frac{1050}{1.05^2} = 999.72.
\]
The difference is small in this simple example, but it becomes material for large portfolios, steep curves, and securities with unusual cash-flow timing.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
section: 3.3 Constructing the Theoretical Spot Rate Curve for Treasuries
text:
3.3 Constructing the Theoretical Spot Rate Curve for Treasuries
The theoretical spot rate curve is the set of zero-coupon Treasury rates implied by Treasury security prices. It is called theoretical because most maturities do not have directly traded zero-coupon Treasury securities.
The curve is usually constructed by bootstrapping:

Use Treasury bills or very short zero-coupon securities to obtain short spot rates directly.
Use the shortest coupon Treasury security to solve for the next spot rate.
Continue maturity by maturity, using previously solved spot rates to discount earlier coupons.

For an annual-pay 2-year coupon Treasury:
\[
P = \frac{C}{1+z_1} + \frac{C+F}{(1+z_2)^2}.
\]
If \(P\), \(C\), \(F\), and \(z_1\) are known, solve for \(z_2\):
\[
z_2 = \left(\frac{C+F}{P - \frac{C}{1+z_1}}\right)^{1/2} - 1.
\]






NoteBootstrapping Example



Assume annual payments and face value $100.



Maturity
Coupon
Price




1 year
0.00%
96.1538


2 years
5.00%
99.4380



The 1-year spot rate is:
\[
z_1 = \frac{100}{96.1538} - 1 = 4.00\%.
\]
For the 2-year bond:
\[
99.4380 = \frac{5}{1.04} + \frac{105}{(1+z_2)^2}.
\]
Solving gives:
\[
z_2 = 5.30\%.
\]










Figure 4: Example of a bootstrapped spot rate curve.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
text:
3.4 On-the-Run Treasury Issues
On-the-run Treasuries are the most recently issued Treasury securities at standard maturities. They are usually the most liquid securities in the Treasury market.
Because they are highly liquid, on-the-run issues often trade at slightly lower yields than older, less liquid Treasury securities with similar maturities. This means the on-the-run curve is useful for market quoting but may embed a liquidity premium.
For example, the current 10-year Treasury note may yield 4.20%, while an older 9.8-year Treasury note may yield 4.25%. The 5 bps difference may reflect liquidity rather than a true difference in risk-free discount rates.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
section: 3.5 All Treasury Coupon Securities and Bills
text:
3.5 All Treasury Coupon Securities and Bills
One approach to constructing the Treasury curve uses all available Treasury bills, notes, and bonds. This approach has more data points than an on-the-run curve.
Advantages:

More observations across maturities.
Less dependence on a small number of benchmark issues.
Better ability to fit a smooth curve.

Challenges:

Different issues may have different liquidity.
Some issues may be rich or cheap due to supply and demand.
Tax and financing effects may affect particular securities.
Coupon effects can make yields difficult to compare directly.

In practice, curve construction often uses statistical fitting methods to smooth observed Treasury prices while controlling for outliers.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
text:
3.6 Treasury Coupon Strips
Treasury STRIPS are securities created by separating Treasury coupon and principal payments into individual zero-coupon instruments. STRIPS provide direct market prices for zero-coupon cash flows.
STRIPS are useful for estimating spot rates because each strip has only one cash flow. However, STRIPS may be less liquid than on-the-run Treasuries and may reflect special supply-demand conditions from pension funds and long-duration investors.






NoteSTRIPS Example



Suppose a Treasury STRIP paying $100 in 10 years trades at $62.00.
The 10-year annual spot rate is:
\[
z_{10} = \left(\frac{100}{62}\right)^{1/10} - 1 = 4.91\%.
\]
Because the STRIP has only one cash flow, its yield is directly interpretable as a spot rate.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
section: 3.7 Using the Theoretical Spot Rate Curve
text:
3.7 Using the Theoretical Spot Rate Curve
The spot rate curve is used to discount each cash flow of a bond at the rate appropriate for that cash-flow date.
For cash flows \(CF_t\) and spot rates \(z_t\):
\[
P = \sum_{t=1}^{n} \frac{CF_t}{(1+z_t)^t}.
\]






NoteSpot Curve Valuation Example



Consider a 3-year annual-pay Treasury with a 4% coupon and face value $100. Assume:



Maturity
Spot rate




1 year
3.50%


2 years
4.00%


3 years
4.40%



The price is:
\[
P = \frac{4}{1.035} + \frac{4}{1.04^2} + \frac{104}{1.044^3} = 98.54.
\]
This price uses the correct discount rate for each cash-flow maturity.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
section: 3.8 Spot Rates and the Base Interest Rate
text:
3.8 Spot Rates and the Base Interest Rate
The base interest rate for a cash flow is best represented by the spot rate for that cash-flow date. A bond’s Treasury benchmark spread can therefore be measured relative to the spot curve rather than a single benchmark maturity.
If a risky bond has cash flows \(CF_t\), its price can be expressed as:
\[
P = \sum_{t=1}^{n} \frac{CF_t}{(1 + z_t + s)^t},
\]
where:

\(z_t\) is the Treasury spot rate for maturity \(t\),
\(s\) is the constant spread over the spot curve.

This spread is conceptually closer to valuation than a simple spread to one Treasury maturity because it respects the timing of each cash flow.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
text:
3.9 Forward Rates
A forward rate is an interest rate implied today for a loan or investment that begins in the future. Forward rates are derived from spot rates.
For annual compounding, the one-year forward rate from year 1 to year 2 is:
\[
1 + f_{1,2} = \frac{(1+z_2)^2}{1+z_1}.
\]
Forward rates are break-even rates. If investors can invest for two years at the 2-year spot rate or invest for one year and then reinvest for another year, the forward rate is the reinvestment rate that makes the two strategies equivalent.






NoteForward Rate Example



Suppose the 1-year spot rate is 4.00% and the 2-year spot rate is 4.80%.
\[
1 + f_{1,2} = \frac{1.048^2}{1.04} = 1.0561.
\]
The one-year forward rate beginning one year from now is 5.61%.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
section: 3.10 Relationship Between Six-Month Forward Rates and Spot Rates
text:
3.10 Relationship Between Six-Month Forward Rates and Spot Rates
Treasury notes and bonds pay semiannual coupons, so six-month rates are especially important.
Let \(z_n\) be the spot rate for maturity \(n\) six-month periods, stated as a six-month periodic rate. The six-month forward rate from period \(n-1\) to period \(n\) is:
\[
1 + f_{n-1,n} = \frac{(1+z_n)^n}{(1+z_{n-1})^{n-1}}.
\]
Equivalently:
\[
f_{n-1,n} = \frac{(1+z_n)^n}{(1+z_{n-1})^{n-1}} - 1.
\]






NoteSix-Month Forward Rate Example



Suppose the 6-month spot rate is 2.00% per half-year and the 1-year spot rate is 2.20% per half-year.
\[
f_{1,2} = \frac{(1.022)^2}{1.020} - 1 = 2.40\%.
\]
The implied six-month rate for the second half-year is 2.40% on a six-month basis.










Figure 5: Forward rates implied by an upward-sloping spot curve.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
text:
3.11 Other Forward Rates
Forward rates can be constructed for any future interval, not only one-year or six-month intervals.
The forward rate from time \(a\) to time \(b\) is:
\[
1 + f_{a,b} =
\left(
\frac{(1+z_b)^b}{(1+z_a)^a}
\right)^{1/(b-a)}.
\]
This formula assumes annual compounding and maturities measured in years.






NoteTwo-Year Forward Rate Beginning Three Years from Now



Suppose the 3-year spot rate is 4.00% and the 5-year spot rate is 4.60%.
\[
1 + f_{3,5} =
\left(
\frac{1.046^5}{1.040^3}
\right)^{1/2}.
\]
The 2-year forward rate beginning in year 3 is 5.51%.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
section: 3.12 Forward Rate as a Hedgeable Rate
text:
3.12 Forward Rate as a Hedgeable Rate
A forward rate is hedgeable when it corresponds to a tradable strategy. For example, an investor can lock in a future borrowing or lending rate using:

Treasury futures,
interest rate swaps,
forward rate agreements,
Eurodollar or SOFR futures,
repo and cash Treasury positions.

The forward rate is not necessarily the market’s forecast of the future spot rate. It is a rate implied by current prices that can often be locked in or hedged.






NoteForward Rate Hedge Example



A pension fund expects to buy a 10-year Treasury note in three months. If the fund is worried that rates will fall before the purchase date, it can buy Treasury futures today. The futures position gains value if rates fall, offsetting the higher cash price of the Treasury note. The hedge converts uncertainty about a future rate into a more predictable effective purchase yield.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
section: 3.13 Determinants of the Shape of the Term Structure
text:
3.13 Determinants of the Shape of the Term Structure
The yield curve shape reflects several forces:

market expectations about future short-term rates,
compensation for interest-rate risk,
investor demand for specific maturities,
supply of securities at different maturities,
central bank policy,
inflation expectations,
economic growth expectations,
safe-haven demand,
balance-sheet and regulatory constraints.

No single theory explains the curve at all times. In practice, the observed curve is the result of expectations, risk premiums, preferred maturity demand, and institutional constraints.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
text:
3.14 Pure Expectations Theory
The pure expectations theory states that forward rates reflect only expected future short-term rates. Under this theory, investors are risk neutral across maturities and do not require a maturity risk premium.
If the yield curve is upward sloping, the theory says the market expects future short-term rates to rise. If the yield curve is inverted, the market expects future short-term rates to fall.
The limitation is that long-term bonds are riskier than rolling short-term bonds, so investors usually require compensation for bearing duration risk.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
text:
3.15 Liquidity Theory
The liquidity theory states that investors prefer shorter maturities because short-term bonds have less price risk and are more liquid. Therefore, long-term bonds must offer a positive liquidity premium.
Under this theory:
\[
\text{Long-term rate} = \text{Expected average future short rates} + \text{Liquidity premium}.
\]
The liquidity premium tends to make the yield curve slope upward even if expected future short rates are unchanged.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
text:
3.16 Preferred Habitat Theory
The preferred habitat theory says investors and borrowers prefer certain maturity ranges but can be induced to move outside those ranges if compensated.
For example:

money market funds prefer short maturities,
banks may prefer intermediate maturities,
pension funds and insurers may prefer long maturities to match liabilities.

If long-maturity investors have strong demand for 30-year bonds, long-term yields may be lower than expectations alone would imply.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
text:
3.17 Market Segmentation Theory
The market segmentation theory is stronger than preferred habitat theory. It says different maturity sectors are largely separate markets, with yields determined by supply and demand in each maturity segment.
For example, the 2-year Treasury yield may be dominated by central bank policy expectations, while the 30-year Treasury yield may be dominated by pension demand, inflation uncertainty, and long-duration supply.
The limitation is that arbitrage and relative-value trading connect maturity sectors, so markets are not completely segmented.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
section: 3.18 The Main Influences on the Shape of the Yield Curve
text:
3.18 The Main Influences on the Shape of the Yield Curve
In practice, the yield curve shape is driven by a combination of macroeconomic and technical forces.







Influence
Typical effect




Expected central bank tightening
Raises short rates; may flatten or invert the curve


Expected central bank easing
Lowers short rates; may steepen the curve


Higher inflation uncertainty
Raises long-term risk premiums


Recession risk
Often lowers intermediate and long rates


Heavy long-term Treasury issuance
Can cheapen long maturities and steepen the curve


Strong pension demand
Can richen long maturities and flatten the long end


Safe-haven demand
Lowers Treasury yields, especially liquid benchmarks











Figure 6: Illustrative effects of macro views on the yield curve.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
text:
5.1 Bull Steepener
A bull steepener is a strategy that benefits when yields fall and short-term yields fall more than long-term yields. This often occurs when the market expects central bank easing.
Example position:

long 2-year Treasury notes,
short 10-year Treasury notes in a duration-adjusted amount.







NoteBull Steepener Example



Suppose the 2-year yield is 4.80% and the 10-year yield is 4.20%. The 2s10s slope is:
\[
4.20\% - 4.80\% = -0.60\%.
\]
The curve is inverted by 60 bps. A trader expects recession risk to rise and the central bank to cut rates. One month later:

2-year yield falls to 4.10%,
10-year yield falls to 3.95%.

The new 2s10s slope is:
\[
3.95\% - 4.10\% = -0.15\%.
\]
The curve steepened by 45 bps. A long 2-year / short 10-year duration-neutral trade profits because the long 2-year position gains more from the larger yield decline than the short 10-year position loses.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
text:
5.2 Bear Steepener
A bear steepener benefits when yields rise and long-term yields rise more than short-term yields. This can occur when inflation risk rises or investors demand a larger term premium.
Example position:

short 30-year Treasury bonds,
long 5-year Treasury notes in a duration-adjusted amount.







NoteBear Steepener Example



The 5-year yield is 4.00% and the 30-year yield is 4.40%, so the 5s30s slope is 40 bps. A trader believes long-term inflation risk is underpriced. Two weeks later:

5-year yield rises to 4.10%,
30-year yield rises to 4.80%.

The 5s30s slope becomes 70 bps. The curve steepened by 30 bps. A short long-bond position gains from the larger yield increase at the long end, while the long 5-year hedge loses less.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
text:
5.3 Bull Flattener
A bull flattener benefits when yields fall and long-term yields fall more than short-term yields. This often occurs when inflation expectations decline or investors seek duration.
Example position:

long 10-year Treasury notes,
short 2-year Treasury notes in a duration-adjusted amount.

If the 10-year yield falls by 50 bps while the 2-year yield falls by only 15 bps, the long 10-year position gains more than the short 2-year position loses.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
text:
5.4 Bear Flattener
A bear flattener benefits when yields rise and short-term yields rise more than long-term yields. This often occurs when the central bank is expected to tighten policy.
Example position:

short 2-year Treasury notes,
long 10-year Treasury notes in a duration-adjusted amount.

If the 2-year yield rises by 75 bps and the 10-year yield rises by 25 bps, the curve flattens. The short 2-year position gains more than the long 10-year position loses.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
text:
5.5 Butterfly Strategy
A butterfly strategy expresses a view on curvature. It compares an intermediate maturity with a weighted average of shorter and longer maturities.
A common 2s5s10s butterfly is:
\[
\text{Butterfly} = 2y_5 - y_2 - y_{10}.
\]
If the 5-year yield is high relative to the 2-year and 10-year yields, the 5-year sector is cheap on the curve. A trader may buy 5-year notes and short 2-year and 10-year notes in duration-adjusted amounts.






NoteButterfly Example



Suppose:



Maturity
Yield




2-year
4.00%


5-year
4.50%


10-year
4.30%



The butterfly is:
\[
2(4.50\%) - 4.00\% - 4.30\% = 0.70\%.
\]
The 5-year point is high relative to the wings. A trader who expects the curve to become smoother may buy the 5-year note and short the 2-year and 10-year notes. If the 5-year yield later falls relative to the wings, the trade profits.










Figure 8: Examples of curve movements relevant for steepener, flattener, and butterfly trades.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
text:
5.6 Carry and Roll-Down
Curve strategies are not driven only by future yield changes. They also earn or lose carry and roll-down.
Carry is the return from holding a position if the yield curve does not change. For a bond, carry includes coupon income minus financing cost.
Roll-down is the price effect from a bond moving to a shorter maturity on an unchanged yield curve. On an upward-sloping curve, a bond may roll down to a lower yield and gain price.






NoteCarry and Roll-Down Example



A 5-year Treasury yields 4.30%. The 4-year point on the curve yields 4.00%. If the curve is unchanged after one year, the bond is now a 4-year bond and its required yield falls by 30 bps. The investor earns coupon income and may also gain from roll-down.
However, if market yields rise enough, the mark-to-market loss can offset the carry and roll-down benefit.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
text:
5.7 Risk Controls in Curve Strategies
Curve strategies should be evaluated with explicit risk controls:

duration exposure,
key rate duration exposure,
convexity exposure,
financing cost,
liquidity risk,
stop-loss levels,
scenario analysis.

A trade that appears to be a curve trade may still lose money if it has unintended exposure to the overall level of rates.






WarningImplementation Risk



A duration-neutral steepener is only neutral for small parallel shifts. It can still lose money if volatility rises, financing conditions change, the curve moves in an unexpected maturity sector, or the hedge instrument does not track the cash bond being hedged.

title: Assignment 1 - Easy
text:
This assignment is based on Lectures 1-6: bond features and risks, pricing and yield measures, duration and convexity, benchmark spreads and term structure, Treasury and corporate debt markets, and residential mortgages/MBS.
The questions are original CFA-style practice questions written from the course material. They are not copied from CFA Institute books or exams.
Questions 1-10 are conceptual, Questions 11-20 are calculations, and Questions 21-25 use the generated spreadsheet files in this folder.


Why does a plain vanilla bond have a predictable cash-flow pattern?
Answer. A plain vanilla bond fixes the coupon rate, coupon dates, face value, and maturity date in the indenture. If the issuer does not default and there is no early redemption, the investor knows both the size and timing of all coupon payments and the final principal repayment. That is why fixed income valuation begins by discounting promised cash flows.



Explain the difference between a fixed-rate bond and a floating-rate note.
Answer. A fixed-rate bond pays the same coupon rate through its life, so its price changes when market yields move away from the coupon. A floating-rate note resets its coupon using a reference rate such as SOFR plus a quoted margin, so its income adjusts with short-term rates. Right after reset, a simple floater often trades close to par if credit spreads are unchanged.



Why does a callable bond usually offer a higher yield than a similar noncallable bond?
Answer. The call option belongs to the issuer and is valuable when rates fall. The issuer can redeem the old high-coupon bond and refinance at lower rates, which limits the investor’s upside and creates reinvestment risk. Investors therefore require extra yield as compensation for giving the issuer that option.



What is credit spread risk?
Answer. Credit spread risk is the risk that the yield spread over a benchmark Treasury or spot curve widens. Even if Treasury rates do not move, a wider spread increases the required yield on the corporate bond and lowers its price. This risk is separate from actual default; a bond can lose value simply because the market demands more compensation for credit or liquidity.



Why should duration not be interpreted as only a measure of time?
Answer. Macaulay duration has time units, but in risk management duration is mainly a measure of price sensitivity to yield changes. Modified duration translates duration into an approximate percentage price change for a small yield change. Two bonds with similar maturities can have very different durations because coupons, yields, and embedded options change the timing and sensitivity of cash flows.



What does positive convexity mean for an option-free bond?
Answer. Positive convexity means the price-yield curve bows outward. For equal-sized yield changes, the price gain when yields fall is larger than the price loss when yields rise. Duration gives the linear first-order effect, while convexity captures the curvature that improves the approximation for larger rate moves.



Why is a spot rate curve better than one yield-to-maturity for valuing a coupon bond?
Answer. A coupon bond has cash flows at many dates. Each cash flow should be discounted at the rate appropriate for its own maturity, so spot rates are conceptually correct. A single yield-to-maturity is a summary discount rate that forces all cash flows to use one rate and can hide errors when the curve is steep or humped.



What is the taxable-equivalent yield of a municipal bond used for?
Answer. It converts a tax-exempt yield into the pretax yield a taxable bond would need to offer to leave the investor equally well off. The formula is tax-exempt yield divided by one minus the marginal tax rate. It matters because investors compare after-tax returns, not only quoted yields.



Why are Treasury bills sold at a discount?
Answer. Treasury bills are zero-coupon securities with maturities of one year or less. They do not pay periodic interest; instead, investors buy them below face value and receive face value at maturity. The difference between purchase price and maturity value is the investor’s interest income.



What is the main risk unique to mortgage-backed securities relative to simple Treasury notes?
Answer. Mortgage-backed securities contain borrower prepayment options. When rates fall, borrowers refinance and return principal early, forcing investors to reinvest at lower yields. When rates rise, prepayments slow and the security extends, leaving investors exposed to a longer-duration asset than expected.



A 3-year annual-pay bond has face value $1,000, a 5% coupon, and a 6% yield. Compute the price.
Answer. The annual coupon is $50. Price = $50/1.06 + $50/1.06^2 + $1,050/1.06^3 = $973.27. Because the coupon rate is below the yield, the bond sells below par.



Compute the price of a 3-year zero-coupon bond with $1,000 face value and a 4% annual yield.
Answer. The only cash flow is the $1,000 maturity payment. Price = $1,000/(1.04)^3 = $889.00.



A quarterly floater pays SOFR + 150 bps. SOFR at reset is 3.50%. Face value is $1,000. What is the next coupon payment?
Answer. The annual coupon rate is 3.50% + 1.50% = 5.00%. Quarterly payment = 5.00%/4 x $1,000 = $12.50.



A semiannual coupon bond pays $25 every six months. Settlement occurs 30 days after the last coupon in a 180-day coupon period. Compute accrued interest.
Answer. Accrued interest = $25 x 30/180 = $4.17. The buyer pays this amount to compensate the seller for interest earned since the last coupon date.



A 5-year corporate bond yields 5.20% and the 5-year Treasury yields 3.90%. Compute the benchmark spread in basis points.
Answer. Spread = 5.20% - 3.90% = 1.30%, or 130 basis points.



A tax-exempt municipal bond yields 3.20%. The investor’s marginal tax rate is 30%. Compute the taxable-equivalent yield.
Answer. Taxable-equivalent yield = 3.20%/(1 - 0.30) = 4.57%. A taxable bond must yield about 4.57% to match the municipal bond after tax.



A 91-day Treasury bill with $10,000 face value is quoted at a 4.75% bank discount yield. Compute the price.
Answer. Price = $10,000 x [1 - 0.0475 x 91/360] = $9,879.93.



A Treasury note is quoted at 98-24. For $1,000 face value, compute the clean price.
Answer. 98-24 means 98 + 24/32 = 98.75% of par. Clean price = 98.7500% x $1,000 = $987.50.



An amortizing security repays principal of $100, $150, $250, and $500 at years 1-4. Compute weighted average life.
Answer. WAL = (100x1 + 150x2 + 250x3 + 500x4)/1,000 = 3.15 years.



Convert a 6% CPR into a single monthly mortality rate.
Answer. SMM = 1 - (1 - 0.06)^(1/12) = 0.5143%. This is the monthly prepayment rate applied after scheduled principal.



Open easy_bond_prices.csv. Use the spreadsheet to compute each bond’s annual coupon dollar amount and decide whether it trades at a discount, premium, or par based only on coupon rate versus yield.
Answer. The coupon dollars are face value multiplied by coupon rate. Bond A: $40 and discount because 4.00% < 5.00%. Bond B: $60 and premium because 6.00% > 4.50%. Bond C: $50 and par because 5.00% = 5.00%.



Open easy_spreads.csv. Use the spreadsheet to compute the spread over Treasury for each issuer in basis points.
Answer. Subtract the Treasury yield from the issuer yield and multiply by 10,000. Agency = 35 bps, Utility = 95 bps, High Yield Industrial = 325 bps. The ranking shows how credit and liquidity risk increase required yield.



Open easy_accrued_interest.csv. Use the spreadsheet to compute accrued interest for each bond.
Answer. Accrued interest equals coupon payment times days since last coupon divided by days in coupon period. Bond A = $6.25, Bond B = $11.67, Bond C = $16.67.



Open easy_mortgage_prepayments.csv. Use the spreadsheet to compute SMM and the expected prepayment for each row.
Answer. For each CPR, SMM = 1 - (1 - CPR)^(1/12), then prepayment = SMM x (beginning balance - scheduled principal). The answers are approximately $2,568, $4,347, and $7,129 for months 1-3.



Open easy_taxable_equivalent.csv. Use the spreadsheet to compute taxable-equivalent yield for each municipal bond.
Answer. Taxable-equivalent yield equals municipal yield divided by one minus the tax rate. The yields are 4.29%, 4.62%, and 5.00%, respectively.

title: Assignment 1 - Medium
text:
This assignment is based on Lectures 1-6: bond features and risks, pricing and yield measures, duration and convexity, benchmark spreads and term structure, Treasury and corporate debt markets, and residential mortgages/MBS.
The questions are original CFA-style practice questions written from the course material. They are not copied from CFA Institute books or exams.
Questions 1-10 are conceptual, Questions 11-20 are calculations, and Questions 21-25 use the generated spreadsheet files in this folder.


A bank portfolio manager says, ‘I prefer floaters because they have no interest-rate risk.’ Evaluate the statement.
Answer. The statement is too strong. Floaters have lower price sensitivity to small parallel shifts shortly after reset because coupons adjust to current short rates, but they still carry spread risk, liquidity risk, cap/floor risk, reset-lag risk, and credit risk. A floater can lose value if the issuer’s required margin widens even when SOFR is unchanged.



Why can a lower-coupon bond have higher duration than a higher-coupon bond with the same maturity?
Answer. Lower coupons push more of the bond’s value into the final principal payment. Because more present value is received later, the weighted average timing of cash flows is later and the price is more sensitive to discount-rate changes. Higher-coupon bonds return more value earlier, which shortens duration.



Explain why pull to par happens when yields are unchanged.
Answer. As maturity approaches, fewer cash flows remain and the principal repayment is less heavily discounted. A discount bond rises toward par because the below-market coupon matters for fewer periods. A premium bond falls toward par because the above-market coupon advantage is being used up.



Why does a callable bond tend to have lower positive convexity than an otherwise identical option-free bond?
Answer. When rates fall, the option-free bond’s price can rise substantially. The callable bond’s price is capped by the increasing probability of being called, so the upside is limited. The issuer’s embedded option therefore subtracts value from the investor and can create negative convexity in the rate region where the call becomes likely.



Distinguish default risk, downgrade risk, and credit spread risk.
Answer. Default risk is failure to make promised payments. Downgrade risk is the risk that a rating agency lowers the issuer’s rating, possibly causing forced selling and higher funding costs. Credit spread risk is the broader market repricing of compensation for credit and liquidity risk; it can occur without default or an actual downgrade.



Why does the on-the-run Treasury curve not always equal the theoretical risk-free discount curve?
Answer. On-the-run Treasuries are the newest and most liquid benchmark issues, so they often trade rich and yield slightly less than comparable seasoned securities. That liquidity premium can contaminate the curve if the goal is pure discounting. A theoretical spot curve tries to infer zero-coupon discount rates across maturities from many prices while controlling for such distortions.



Explain the economic meaning of a forward rate derived from spot rates.
Answer. A forward rate is the break-even reinvestment rate implied by today’s spot rates. If the forward rate from year 1 to year 2 is 5.6%, an investor is indifferent, before risk premiums, between investing for two years directly and investing for one year then reinvesting for the second year at that forward rate. It is not automatically a forecast; it can include term and liquidity premiums.



Why do market-cap-weighted bond indexes have a structural weakness?
Answer. They give the largest weights to the largest borrowers, not necessarily to the safest or most attractive issuers. A heavily indebted issuer can become a larger benchmark constituent precisely because it has issued more debt. This creates an incentive for benchmark-aware managers to hold more exposure to large debtors unless they actively deviate.



Why is average life important for a mortgage pool but insufficient by itself?
Answer. Average life summarizes the weighted timing of principal repayments, which is useful for comparing mortgage pools with prepayments. But two pools can share the same average life while having different month-by-month cash-flow distributions, prepayment convexity, and extension risk. Investors need the full cash-flow path, not only one summary statistic.



What makes a leveraged loan different from a high-yield bond?
Answer. Leveraged loans usually have floating rates, are often senior secured, and sit higher in the capital structure. High-yield bonds usually have fixed coupons, longer maturities, and may be unsecured. The loan has less rate duration but still has credit, liquidity, covenant, and refinancing risk.



A 6-year bond has $1,000 face value, 6% annual coupon paid semiannually, and a 5.20% yield. Compute the price.
Answer. Semiannual coupon = $30, semiannual yield = 2.60%, and there are 12 periods. Price = sum of discounted coupons plus principal = $1,040.78. The bond trades above par because its coupon rate exceeds its yield.



Compute Macaulay and modified duration for a 4-year annual-pay 5% coupon bond yielding 6%.
Answer. Using present-value weights for the four cash flows, Macaulay duration is 3.718 years. Modified duration = Macaulay duration/(1 + y) = 3.507. A 1 bp rise in yield lowers price by roughly 0.0351%.



For the bond in Question 12, use modified duration and convexity to approximate the percentage price change for a 75 bp yield increase.
Answer. Convexity is approximately 16.133. The approximation is -3.507 x 0.0075 + 0.5 x 16.133 x 0.0075^2 = -2.585%. Dollar change is about -24.96.



A 5-year annual-pay bond has a 4% coupon and 5.50% yield. Compute price and identify discount or premium.
Answer. Price = $935.95. It is a discount bond because the coupon rate is lower than the required yield.



Price a 3-year annual-pay 4% Treasury with $1,000 face value using spot rates of 3.50%, 4.00%, and 4.50%.
Answer. Price = $40/1.035 + $40/1.04^2 + $1,040/1.045^3 = $986.98. Each cash flow is discounted at the spot rate matching its date.

title: Assignment 1 - Medium
text:
This assignment is based on Lectures 1-6: bond features and risks, pricing and yield measures, duration and convexity, benchmark spreads and term structure, Treasury and corporate debt markets, and residential mortgages/MBS.
The questions are original CFA-style practice questions written from the course material. They are not copied from CFA Institute books or exams.
Questions 1-10 are conceptual, Questions 11-20 are calculations, and Questions 21-25 use the generated spreadsheet files in this folder.


A bank portfolio manager says, ‘I prefer floaters because they have no interest-rate risk.’ Evaluate the statement.
Answer. The statement is too strong. Floaters have lower price sensitivity to small parallel shifts shortly after reset because coupons adjust to current short rates, but they still carry spread risk, liquidity risk, cap/floor risk, reset-lag risk, and credit risk. A floater can lose value if the issuer’s required margin widens even when SOFR is unchanged.



Why can a lower-coupon bond have higher duration than a higher-coupon bond with the same maturity?
Answer. Lower coupons push more of the bond’s value into the final principal payment. Because more present value is received later, the weighted average timing of cash flows is later and the price is more sensitive to discount-rate changes. Higher-coupon bonds return more value earlier, which shortens duration.



Explain why pull to par happens when yields are unchanged.
Answer. As maturity approaches, fewer cash flows remain and the principal repayment is less heavily discounted. A discount bond rises toward par because the below-market coupon matters for fewer periods. A premium bond falls toward par because the above-market coupon advantage is being used up.



Why does a callable bond tend to have lower positive convexity than an otherwise identical option-free bond?
Answer. When rates fall, the option-free bond’s price can rise substantially. The callable bond’s price is capped by the increasing probability of being called, so the upside is limited. The issuer’s embedded option therefore subtracts value from the investor and can create negative convexity in the rate region where the call becomes likely.



Distinguish default risk, downgrade risk, and credit spread risk.
Answer. Default risk is failure to make promised payments. Downgrade risk is the risk that a rating agency lowers the issuer’s rating, possibly causing forced selling and higher funding costs. Credit spread risk is the broader market repricing of compensation for credit and liquidity risk; it can occur without default or an actual downgrade.



Why does the on-the-run Treasury curve not always equal the theoretical risk-free discount curve?
Answer. On-the-run Treasuries are the newest and most liquid benchmark issues, so they often trade rich and yield slightly less than comparable seasoned securities. That liquidity premium can contaminate the curve if the goal is pure discounting. A theoretical spot curve tries to infer zero-coupon discount rates across maturities from many prices while controlling for such distortions.



Explain the economic meaning of a forward rate derived from spot rates.
Answer. A forward rate is the break-even reinvestment rate implied by today’s spot rates. If the forward rate from year 1 to year 2 is 5.6%, an investor is indifferent, before risk premiums, between investing for two years directly and investing for one year then reinvesting for the second year at that forward rate. It is not automatically a forecast; it can include term and liquidity premiums.



Why do market-cap-weighted bond indexes have a structural weakness?
Answer. They give the largest weights to the largest borrowers, not necessarily to the safest or most attractive issuers. A heavily indebted issuer can become a larger benchmark constituent precisely because it has issued more debt. This creates an incentive for benchmark-aware managers to hold more exposure to large debtors unless they actively deviate.

Answer. Average life summarizes the weighted timing of principal repayments, which is useful for comparing mortgage pools with prepayments. But two pools can share the same average life while having different month-by-month cash-flow distributions, prepayment convexity, and extension risk. Investors need the full cash-flow path, not only one summary statistic.

Answer. Leveraged loans usually have floating rates, are often senior secured, and sit higher in the capital structure. title: Assignment 1 - Hard
text:
This assignment is based on Lectures 1-6: bond features and risks, pricing and yield measures, duration and convexity, benchmark spreads and term structure, Treasury and corporate debt markets, and residential mortgages/MBS.
The questions are original CFA-style practice questions written from the course material. They are not copied from CFA Institute books or exams.
Questions 1-10 are conceptual, Questions 11-20 are calculations, and Questions 21-25 use the generated spreadsheet files in this folder.


A CIO argues that the safest way to reduce risk is to buy the highest-yielding bonds with the shortest maturities. Give a deep critique.
Answer. Short maturity reduces exposure to level changes in rates, but high yield is often compensation for credit distress, weak liquidity, poor covenants, or near-term refinancing risk. A very short distressed bond can be more dangerous than a longer high-quality bond because the main risk is not duration; it is whether the issuer survives the maturity wall. The correct risk question is which factor is being paid for and whether the spread is enough after expected default loss, downgrade risk, liquidity cost, and portfolio constraints.



Why can a bond’s yield-to-maturity be a misleading measure of expected return?
Answer. YTM assumes promised cash flows are paid, coupons are reinvested at the same yield, and the bond is held to maturity. Those assumptions fail for callable bonds, mortgage-backed securities, distressed bonds, and investors with shorter horizons. Expected return must incorporate reinvestment rates, future sale yield, default probability, recovery, taxes, and embedded option exercise.



Explain why convexity is economically valuable even if two bonds have the same duration and yield.
Answer. If two option-free bonds have the same duration and yield, the more convex bond has a more favorable response to rate volatility: larger gains when yields fall and smaller losses when yields rise. Convexity is valuable because it improves the distribution of price changes. Investors often accept lower yield for more convexity, while callable mortgages may offer more yield because they sell convexity to borrowers.



A portfolio has the same effective duration as its benchmark. Why can it still lose heavily relative to the benchmark when the curve twists?
Answer. Effective duration summarizes sensitivity to a parallel shift. A curve twist changes short, intermediate, and long rates by different amounts. If the portfolio is overweight long key-rate duration and underweight intermediate key-rate duration relative to the benchmark, the same total duration can hide a major mismatch. Key rate duration is needed to expose that curve-shape risk.



Give an intuition for why a theoretical spot curve is a set of discount rates, not a set of expected future short rates.
Answer. Spot rates are today’s prices for zero-coupon cash flows at each maturity. They embed time value, risk premiums, liquidity, financing specialness, and supply-demand effects. Forward rates extracted from spot rates are break-even rates under no-arbitrage pricing, but they are not pure forecasts unless risk premiums are zero and investors are risk-neutral.



Why can a wider spread be rational for a more liquid corporate bond in stressed markets?
Answer. Normally liquidity lowers required yield. In stress, the most liquid bond may be the one investors sell first because it can actually trade, causing its spread to widen faster than illiquid bonds whose prices are stale. The observed spread can therefore reflect immediacy, balance-sheet pressure, and mark-to-market activity, not only fundamental credit deterioration.



Explain the investor’s hidden short option position in a mortgage pass-through.
Answer. The mortgage borrower owns the right to prepay. The MBS investor has effectively sold that option because principal returns when it is least convenient: faster when rates fall and reinvestment yields are low, slower when rates rise and the investor would prefer principal back. This produces negative convexity and makes duration state-dependent.



Why is ‘risk risk’ especially relevant for structured fixed-income products?
Answer. Structured products can transform simple loans into tranches with nonlinear exposure to default timing, prepayments, volatility, liquidity, and correlation. A yield pickup may look attractive if the investor models only average loss or average life, while ignoring tail behavior and option exposure. Risk risk is the danger of owning a payoff the investor cannot actually explain under stress scenarios.



How can bond covenants transfer value between shareholders and bondholders?
Answer. Shareholders benefit from risk-taking because upside is theirs while part of downside is borne by creditors. Negative covenants restrict actions such as additional debt, asset sales, or dividend leakage that would weaken bondholder claims. Strong covenants reduce agency conflict and can lower required spreads; weak covenants leave bondholders exposed to value transfer.



Why is leverage in a bond portfolio conceptually different from simply buying longer-duration bonds?
Answer. Both can increase rate exposure, but leverage also introduces financing risk, margin calls, haircut changes, repo rollover risk, and forced-sale risk. A long-duration unlevered Treasury position can suffer mark-to-market losses, but a levered position can become insolvent or be liquidated at bad prices even if the long-run thesis is correct. The financing channel is therefore a separate risk factor.



A pension analyst studies an 8-year semiannual-pay corporate bond with $1,000 face value and 4.75% coupon. The current yield is 5.25%. Reprice the bond when yield is 4.75% and 5.75%, then estimate empirical modified duration and convexity using a 50 bp shock.

Answer. Using the three prices, empirical modified duration = (P_minus - P_plus)/(2 x P0 x 0.005) = 6.553. Empirical convexity = (P_minus + P_plus - 2P0)/(P0 x 0.005^2) = 51.03. The duration is the first-order exposure, while the convexity shows the curvature becomes material for larger shocks.

Maturity

Compute the present value of the 5-year liability using the correct rate.
Answer. The liability is a single 5-year cash flow, so it should be discounted at the 5-year spot rate, not an average curve yield. PV = $2,700,000/(1.047)^5 = $2,146,003.15.



A 4-year annual-pay corporate bond has a 3.50% coupon and $1,000 face value. The Treasury spot curve is:



Year

Compute the Treasury-curve value before adding any credit spread.
Answer. Discount each cash flow at the matching spot rate. Price = 35/1.032 + 35/1.039^2 + 35/1.046^3 + 1,035/1.052^4 = $941.96. This is the value if the risky bond required only Treasury spot rates.



Using the spot rates in Question 13, compute the annual forward rate from year 2 to year 4.
Answer. 1 + f_2,4 = [(1.052)4/(1.039)2]^(1/2). The two-year forward rate beginning in year 2 is 6.52%. It is the break-even two-year rate for years 3 and 4.



A 5-year high-yield bond has cumulative default probability of 18% and expected recovery of 45% of par. Approximate the annual expected credit loss spread using a simple straight-line method.
Answer. Expected cumulative loss = default probability x loss given default = 18% x (1 - 45%) = 9.90%. Straight-line annual compensation is about 1.98%, or 198 bps, before liquidity, risk premium, and timing effects.



An investor in the 37% tax bracket compares a 5.60% taxable corporate bond with a 3.80% tax-exempt municipal bond. Which has the higher after-tax yield?
Answer. Corporate after-tax yield = 5.60% x (1 - 37%) = 3.53%. The municipal yield is 3.80% tax exempt. The municipal bond has the higher after-tax yield by 27 bps, before considering credit and liquidity differences.



A Treasury note position has $1,000,000 face value, quoted clean at 100-16+, and semiannual coupon payment of $22,500. Settlement is 42 days into a 182-day coupon period. Compute full settlement price.
Answer. 100-16+ = 100 + 16/32 + 1/64 = 100.515625% of par. Clean dollars = $1,005,156.25. Accrued interest = $22,500 x 42/182 = $5,192.31. Full price = $1,010,348.56.



A new agency mortgage pool follows 100% PSA for the first six months. Beginning balance is $500,000, and scheduled principal is $900 per month. Under 100% PSA, CPR is 0.2% in month 1, 0.4% in month 2, and rises by 0.2% monthly. Compute the month-6 ending balance.
Assume prepayment each month is SMM x (beginning balance - scheduled principal).
Answer. Applying the PSA ramp monthly gives an ending balance of approximately $492,859.15 after month 6. The balance declines by scheduled principal plus increasing prepayments as CPR ramps up.



An investor buys a bond for $990, receives a $40 coupon after one year, reinvests nothing because the horizon is one year, and sells the bond for $1,010. Compute one-year horizon return.
Answer. Total dollar return = coupon + price change = $40 + ($1,010 - $990) = $60. Horizon return = $60/$990 = 7.27%. This differs from YTM because it uses the realized sale price and actual horizon.



A leveraged fund buys $10,000,000 of agency debt yielding 5.20%, finances it in repo at 4.40%, pays 20 bps annual operating/friction cost on assets, and faces an 8% haircut. Approximate return on equity before price changes.
Answer. Net carry dollars = (5.20% - 4.40% - 0.20%) x $10,000,000 = $60,000. Equity tied up by the haircut is 8% x $10,000,000 = $800,000. Approximate ROE = $60,000/$800,000 = 7.50%. The number is attractive only if financing remains available and spreads do not widen.



Open hard_curve_trade.csv. The portfolio manager expects a bear flattening: 2-year rates +80 bps, 5-year rates +55 bps, 10-year rates +25 bps, and 30-year rates +10 bps. Use the key-rate dollar durations to estimate each portfolio’s dollar P&L and choose the less exposed portfolio.
Answer. Multiply each key-rate dollar duration by the rate shock in basis points and sum the negatives. Portfolio Alpha loses about $972,500; Portfolio Beta loses about $755,000. Beta is less exposed because it has less short/intermediate key-rate exposure where the shock is largest.



Open hard_callable_vs_noncallable.csv. Using the scenario prices, compute effective duration for the callable and noncallable bonds. Explain the difference.
Answer. Effective duration = (P_down - P_up)/(2 x P0 x shock). The noncallable bond has duration about 7.52, while the callable bond has duration about 3.52. The callable bond’s upside price is capped when rates fall, so its effective duration and convexity are lower around the call region.



Open hard_credit_expected_loss.csv. Compute expected loss in dollars for each bond, loss-adjusted spread in bps, and identify which bond has the best spread per unit of expected loss.
Answer. Expected loss = exposure x default probability x (1 - recovery). The approximate expected losses are $132,000, $112,000, and $135,000. Loss-adjusted spread is quoted spread minus annualized expected loss as a percent of exposure; Bond C is strongest on this simple measure because its quoted spread remains much wider after subtracting expected loss. This does not mean Bond C is automatically best, because tail risk, liquidity, and downgrade risk still matter.



Open hard_mbs_waterfall.csv. Use the mortgage-pool data to compute SMM, prepayment, total principal, ending balance, and average life contribution for each month.
Answer. The method is month-by-month: convert CPR to SMM, compute prepayment after scheduled principal, total principal, and ending balance. Summing month x total principal divided by original balance gives the partial average-life contribution for the first six months, approximately 0.014 years; most principal remains outstanding beyond the displayed horizon.



Open hard_immunization.csv. Use the asset and liability cash-flow tables to compute present value and Macaulay duration at the given spot rates. Determine whether the asset portfolio is immunized.
Answer. Discount each cash flow using the matching spot rate. The asset PV is about $10.15 million and asset Macaulay duration is about 4.55 years. Liability PV is about $9.60 million and liability duration is about 5.10 years. The portfolio has more present value than the liabilities but is under-duration relative to them, so it is not fully immunized against small parallel shifts.

A 5-year high-yield bond has cumulative default probability of 18% and expected recovery of 45% of par. Approximate the annual expected credit loss spread using a simple straight-line method.
Answer. Expected cumulative loss = default probability x loss given default = 18% x (1 - 45%) = 9.90%. Straight-line annual compensation is about 1.98%, or 198 bps, before liquidity, risk premium, and timing effects.



An investor in the 37% tax bracket compares a 5.60% taxable corporate bond with a 3.80% tax-exempt municipal bond. Which has the higher after-tax yield?
Answer. Corporate after-tax yield = 5.60% x (1 - 37%) = 3.53%. The municipal yield is 3.80% tax exempt. The municipal bond has the higher after-tax yield by 27 bps, before considering credit and liquidity differences.



A Treasury note position has $1,000,000 face value, quoted clean at 100-16+, and semiannual coupon payment of $22,500. Settlement is 42 days into a 182-day coupon period. Compute full settlement price.
Answer. 100-16+ = 100 + 16/32 + 1/64 = 100.515625% of par. Clean dollars = $1,005,156.25. Accrued interest = $22,500 x 42/182 = $5,192.31. Full price = $1,010,348.56.



A new agency mortgage pool follows 100% PSA for the first six months. Beginning balance is $500,000, and scheduled principal is $900 per month. Under 100% PSA, CPR is 0.2% in month 1, 0.4% in month 2, and rises by 0.2% monthly. Compute the month-6 ending balance.
Assume prepayment each month is SMM x (beginning balance - scheduled principal).
Answer. Applying the PSA ramp monthly gives an ending balance of approximately $492,859.15 after month 6. The balance declines by scheduled principal plus increasing prepayments as CPR ramps up.



An investor buys a bond for $990, receives a $40 coupon after one year, reinvests nothing because the horizon is one year, and sells the bond for $1,010. Compute one-year horizon return.
Answer. Total dollar return = coupon + price change = $40 + ($1,010 - $990) = $60. Horizon return = $60/$990 = 7.27%. This differs from YTM because it uses the realized sale price and actual horizon.



A leveraged fund buys $10,000,000 of agency debt yielding 5.20%, finances it in repo at 4.40%, pays 20 bps annual operating/friction cost on assets, and faces an 8% haircut. Approximate return on equity before price changes.
Answer. Net carry dollars = (5.20% - 4.40% - 0.20%) x $10,000,000 = $60,000. Equity tied up by the haircut is 8% x $10,000,000 = $800,000. Approximate ROE = $60,000/$800,000 = 7.50%. The number is attractive only if financing remains available and spreads do not widen.



Open hard_curve_trade.csv. The portfolio manager expects a bear flattening: 2-year rates +80 bps, 5-year rates +55 bps, 10-year rates +25 bps, and 30-year rates +10 bps. Use the key-rate dollar durations to estimate each portfolio’s dollar P&L and choose the less exposed portfolio.
Answer. Multiply each key-rate dollar duration by the rate shock in basis points and sum the negatives. Portfolio Alpha loses about $972,500; Portfolio Beta loses about $755,000. Beta is less exposed because it has less short/intermediate key-rate exposure where the shock is largest.



Open hard_callable_vs_noncallable.csv. Using the scenario prices, compute effective duration for the callable and noncallable bonds. Explain the difference.
Answer. Effective duration = (P_down - P_up)/(2 x P0 x shock). The noncallable bond has duration about 7.52, while the callable bond has duration about 3.52. The callable bond’s upside price is capped when rates fall, so its effective duration and convexity are lower around the call region.



Open hard_credit_expected_loss.csv. Compute expected loss in dollars for each bond, loss-adjusted spread in bps, and identify which bond has the best spread per unit of expected loss.
Answer. Expected loss = exposure x default probability x (1 - recovery). The approximate expected losses are $132,000, $112,000, and $135,000. Loss-adjusted spread is quoted spread minus annualized expected loss as a percent of exposure; Bond C is strongest on this simple measure because its quoted spread remains much wider after subtracting expected loss. This does not mean Bond C is automatically best, because tail risk, liquidity, and downgrade risk still matter.



Open hard_mbs_waterfall.csv. Use the mortgage-pool data to compute SMM, prepayment, total principal, ending balance, and average life contribution for each month.
Answer. The method is month-by-month: convert CPR to SMM, compute prepayment after scheduled principal, total principal, and ending balance. Summing month x total principal divided by original balance gives the partial average-life contribution for the first six months, approximately 0.014 years; most principal remains outstanding beyond the displayed horizon.



Open hard_immunization.csv. Use the asset and liability cash-flow tables to compute present value and Macaulay duration at the given spot rates. Determine whether the asset portfolio is immunized.
Answer. Discount each cash flow using the matching spot rate. The asset PV is about $10.15 million and asset Macaulay duration is about 4.55 years. Liability PV is about $9.60 million and liability duration is about 5.10 years. The portfolio has more present value than the liabilities but is under-duration relative to them, so it is not fully immunized against small parallel shifts.
